segments.title: From Ernest Appert to Laïd Sebaï
segments.text:
Leave number twenty-one behind now, and walk gently along the street.

We haven't far to go.

But in those few steps, we're going to move forward almost a century.

Leave the nineteenth-century photography studios behind.

We're entering the Paris of the nineteen seventies.

The grand old façades are still standing.

But the life behind them has changed completely.

There are offices on the upper floors. Associations occupy other rooms. People arrive to work in the morning and leave again in the evening.

And some entrances still conceal courtyards and hallways that passers-by never see.

Look now at the large grey carriage doorway at number twenty-three.

Notice its two leaves, the carved decoration and the stone surround.

Building work here is documented in eighteen eighty-three and eighteen eighty-four.

We don't yet know exactly when the doors you can see were made.

But this entrance is an unmistakable landmark in the street.

In December nineteen seventy-seven, newspaper reports gave the address of the Amicale des Algériens en Europe as number twenty-three bis.

We cannot yet say with certainty which precise entrance that designation referred to.

The uncertainty about the doorway remains.

But the events themselves are coming into focus.

On the morning of Friday, the second of December, nineteen seventy-seven, a man was finishing his shift as a night watchman somewhere behind one of these entrances.

He was still inside the building.

The street was beginning to wake up.

He would soon be leaving.

But he would never make it home.

At the end of this short walk, we can finally give him his name.

Laïd Sebaï.

This is his story.
